opus-5.5.text:
Oh, that exam, I still remember it really clearly. Coming into Tsinghua, I thought of myself as someone who was pretty good at math. In high school I could usually solve problems quickly, and I was confident. Then I sat down for that first exam and realized very quickly that I didn't know how to approach a lot of the problems. It wasn't the kind of math where you plug things into a formula. It was proofs, abstraction, discrete structures, the kind of rigorous thinking I hadn't really trained for.

I remember staring at the paper and feeling time slip away. I'd write something, cross it out, try another direction, and nothing clicked. When the results came back, my score was much lower than I expected. It was humbling. Tsinghua is full of extremely talented people, and suddenly you're not the smartest person in the room anymore. Some of my classmates seemed to handle it effortlessly, and I couldn't understand how.

Looking back, the frustration was useful. It forced me to admit that my understanding was shallow in places, and that being "good at math" in high school was a different skill from thinking like a mathematician or a computer scientist. I had to change how I studied. I needed to really understand why things worked instead of just memorizing techniques. That shift ended up shaping how I approached research later, especially in graphics and simulation, where you need solid foundations to build anything meaningful. So it was painful at the time, but it was one of those experiences that made me grow.

fable-5.1.text:
Oh, that exam. I still remember it, honestly, because it was the first time at Tsinghua where I walked out of a room feeling like I had completely misjudged myself.

I came in pretty confident. I'd done competitive programming in high school, I was used to being the person who finished early, and I figured applied math would just be a formality on the way to the interesting stuff, which for me was always graphics and simulation. So I prepared the way I'd prepare for a programming contest. I practiced problem types, I memorized the shape of the solutions, I assumed if I'd seen something similar I could reproduce it.

Then the exam came and the problems weren't like that at all. They weren't asking me to reproduce a procedure. They were asking whether I actually understood why the procedure worked. There was a question on probability, I think, where I knew the formula perfectly and I just couldn't see which formula applied, because I'd never really asked myself what the formula meant. I sat there for maybe twenty minutes on one problem, rewriting the same thing, getting nowhere, and I could hear other people turning pages around me.

What made it frustrating wasn't the score. The score was mediocre, not a disaster. It was the feeling of running the same mental loop over and over and knowing it wasn't going to converge. As a programmer you're used to being able to debug. You print something, you narrow it down. But here I couldn't even locate where my understanding had broken, because it had never really been there in the first place. That's a very specific kind of helplessness.

In hindsight I'm grateful for it, because it changed how I learn. After that I stopped treating math as a toolbox I could pull things out of and started treating it as something I had to actually rebuild in my own head, derive things myself, ask the dumb "but why" questions. That habit ended up mattering a lot later, when I was working on physical simulation and Taichi, because there you're constantly hitting things where no one has written the recipe yet. But at nineteen, sitting in that exam hall, it just felt like being stuck in a loop with no exit.
